issues.legal_issue: A claim of private defence and unexplained injuries to an accused do not defeat a prosecution case when the accused fails to establish the circumstances requiring defensive force and the prosecution evidence is clear and credible.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the deceased and his relatives began the fight and that the accused acted in private defence.
The accused relied on a counter-report that was not proved at trial and called no defence witnesses to establish their account of the incident.
One accused had injuries, but the medical evidence described them as simple, and the prosecution account was supported by credible eyewitness testimony.
issues.conclusion: The private-defence claim was not established, and the failure to explain the accused’s injuries did not create a reasonable doubt or undermine the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: The accused who claims private defence must establish the basic circumstances and occasion for exercising that right, and defensive force must be proportionate to the aggression. Although the prosecution should ordinarily explain injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence, non-explanation does not automatically defeat the case; it materially affects the prosecution only where the injuries were serious and were sustained at the time of the occurrence. Clear, cogent and creditworthy prosecution evidence may be accepted despite unexplained injuries. The Court relied on Rajender Singh v. State of Bihar, (2000) 4 SCC 298; Ram Sunder Yadav v. State of Bihar, (1998) 7 SCC 365; and Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P., (1990) 3 SCC 190.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and private_defence_claimed and accused_failed_to_establish_aggression and accused_injuries_were_simple and prosecution_evidence_was_clear_and_credible

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.private_defence_claimed: The accused said that they used force to defend themselves against an attack by the deceased or the deceased’s companions.
predicates.accused_failed_to_establish_aggression: The accused did not establish facts showing that the deceased or the deceased’s companions were the aggressors or that defensive force was necessary.
predicates.accused_injuries_were_simple: The medical evidence described the accused’s injuries as simple rather than serious.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_was_clear_and_credi: The prosecution presented evidence that the court found clear, credible and sufficient to distinguish the true account of the incident.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a conviction after claiming private defence, simple injuries to the accused and a failure to establish the alleged aggression do not displace a conviction supported by clear and credible prosecution evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Credible testimony from related or injured eyewitnesses can support a conviction, and the non-examination of independent witnesses, another injured witness or the investigating officer is not necessarily fatal to the prosecution case.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on eyewitnesses who were relatives of the deceased, including one eyewitness who had been injured in the occurrence.
The injured eyewitness’s account was found cogent and reliable and was supported by medical and other evidence.
Another injured person and independent villagers were not examined, and the investigating officer was not produced.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship to the deceased and the non-examination of other witnesses or the investigating officer did not undermine the prosecution case, because the evidence relied upon was credible and corroborated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 134 of the Evidence Act, 1872 does not require a particular number of witnesses; the quality and credibility of evidence, rather than its quantity, govern. Relationship to the victim alone does not make a witness interested or unreliable. An injured witness has a special evidentiary status because the injury supports the witness’s presence at the scene, and the testimony should be relied upon absent strong grounds for rejection. The prosecution need not always examine the investigating officer if it proves its case beyond reasonable doubt without that evidence. The Court relied on Namdeo v. State of Maharashtra, (2007) 14 SCC 150; Satbir Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2009) 13 SCC 790; Balraje v. State of Maharashtra, (2010) 6 SCC 673; Abdul Sayeed v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2010) 10 SCC 259; and Anil Phukan v. State of Assam, (1993) 3 SCC 282.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.related_or_injured_eyewitness_testimony_: A relative of the victim or a witness injured in the occurrence gave testimony that the court found reliable.
predicates.testimony_was_corroborated: The eyewitness testimony was supported by other oral, medical or documentary evidence.
predicates.other_witnesses_or_investigator_were_not: The prosecution did not call one or more available independent or injured witnesses, or did not examine the investigating officer.

issues.definition: When credible eyewitness testimony is corroborated, the conviction can stand even though other witnesses or the investigating officer were not examined.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-planned attack carried out with common intention can sustain joint liability for murder even without proof of a distinct overt act by each accused or an unlawful assembly of five or more persons.
material_facts: The accused returned to the disputed location armed with lathis after an earlier exchange about earth being placed on the land.
They gave a call to kill the deceased and attacked him together, causing injuries that medical evidence found ordinarily sufficient to cause death.

The evidence supported the finding that the attack was planned and that the participants acted with a common intention; fewer than five accused remained for consideration after other accused were acquitted.
The court found the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and rejected the contention that the incident was a sudden fight warranting a lesser homicide conviction.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for murder with the aid of common intention was affirmed, and the request to reduce the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, participants who commit murder in furtherance of a common intention may be held jointly liable; the extent of each participant’s overt act does not determine liability where common intention and participation are established. Section 34 does not require an unlawful assembly of five or more persons. The Court relied on Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1961 SC 1787, and distinguished Marimuthu v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2008) 3 SCC 205, because the attack was not a fight arising at the spur of the moment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_murder_conviction and accused_returned_prepared_and_armed and accused_attacked_together_with_common_intention and attack_caused_fatal_injuries

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_murder_convictio: The accused appealed a conviction for murder.
predicates.accused_returned_prepared_and_armed: The accused returned to the scene prepared to use weapons against the victim.
predicates.accused_attacked_together_with_common_in: The accused acted together pursuant to a shared intention to attack the victim.
predicates.attack_caused_fatal_injuries: The attack caused injuries that resulted in the victim’s death and were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course.

issues.definition: When accused appealing a murder conviction return prepared and armed, act together with a common intention, and cause fatal injuries, their joint murder conviction can be sustained.
